
Forecasters attempting to predict infectious disease outbreaks have met with varying success [@]. 
This variation may be because of varying predictive power among forecasting methods, or because of varying difficulty among forecast tasks.
To evaluate the contribution of these two factors in predictive performance, we need a comparable sample of many independent forecasting models across many forecast tasks [(10)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?8yn1XI)[(11)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ZgO6IM).
This comparability is achieved in participatory forecast challenges [(13)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?7pIGoa).
Yet even with comparable evaluation between models, the relative contribution of factors influencing performance has not been well identified.
Identifying these influences on performance is important in order to fairly evaluate between different forecasters, and to set appropriate expectations for performance between different forecast settings.

Among many forecasters, some variation in performance may be attributed to the variety of structural approaches to developing a forecasting model. 
Forecasters may choose among many methods in model development. 
This might range from purely data-driven statistical methods, to mechanistic models that embed explicit hypotheses about biological or epidemiological drivers of transmission. 
Different structural approaches may be better suited to different purposes, for example scenario projection, policy analysis, or real-time nowcasting. 
This choice demands a trade-off among complementary strengths and weaknesses of different methods [(1–3)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?XemggF), any of which may impact predictive accuracy.
Previous work has compared predictive performance between these approaches, and shown little evidence for substantial differences[(4–6)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?piAg9a).
However, evaluations typically summarise performance across many forecast tasks simultaneously.
This means that comparisons may conflate differences in the predictive performance of each structural approach, with parallel differences in forecast task difficulty.

Variation in forecast task difficulty is also a factor in forecast performance. 
We see better predictive performance when the forecast task is short term [(15)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?2K90bo), with stable epidemic dynamics [(9)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?KaFMKc), in larger populations [(16)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?7uCfbD), with timely surveillance [(6)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?YLVYXN), or with informative leading indicators [(17)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?gzkBxT). 
At the same time, there may be inherent limits to infectious disease predictability [(14)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?CZumUU). 
Evaluating forecasts across multiple forecast tasks should therefore account for task difficulty, before comparing other factors influencing predictive performance. 
This is typically accounted for qualitatively, based on knowledge of varying forecasting contexts [@sherratt]. 
Few evaluations have explicitly accounted for task difficulty-related variables using more formal analytical methods.

Such analysis is challenging as it is prone to selection bias, confounding, and interaction effects (effect modification) when evaluating among forecasters with differential participation across forecast tasks. 
One potential such interaction is where the effect of model structure is modified by a forecaster's strategy for selecting forecasting tasks. 
This strategy may influence structural approach to model development, their ability to participate in different forecast tasks, and their resulting predictive performance.
Faced with multiple forecasting tasks, a forecaster might produce forecasts for any given task given only updated data, as is typical of statistical time-series and many semi-mechanistic models.
An alternative strategy is to develop a model to a specific forecast task, for example emphasising particular mechanistic processes or exploiting local data sources. 
Bespoke mechanistic models are more easily tailored to a single task in this way [(7,8)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?vo794b). 
A study of COVID-19 forecasts in Germany and Poland found the two best-performing models were those specifically tuned to the national context [(9)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?7QAdmm).
This suggests the hypothesis that task participation has a separate influence on predictive performance, and could confound an estimate of the effect of model structure on predictive performance.

Here, we develop a framework to identify the partial effect of model structure on predictive performance, while jointly adjusting for forecast task difficulty and task participation. 
We include a directed acyclic graph in the Supplement to represent our assumed causal structure, but note that our work is exploratory rather than formally causal.
We apply this framework to evaluate short-term forecasts of COVID-19 across Europe, using proper scoring rules to evaluate forecasts and using a generalised additive mixed model to associate this with model structure, factors influencing task difficulty, and task participation.
We find that, despite superficial differences between model structures, most of the variation in observed performance can be explained by factors associated with forecast task difficulty. 
We do not have the ability to fully test our assumptions, and we consider directions for a fuller causal treatment in future work.
